name: L'Arpège
tier: THE BERTHS · LA CRÈME — THE THREE-STAR HOUSES
recognition: Three MICHELIN Stars, Guide MICHELIN France 2026
what_to_order: Tomato mosaic|Flambéed aubergine with melon confit|Onion, carrot, shallot and cabbage|Garden crudités
price_range: Call ahead: Gault&Millau 2026 gives EUR 260-420 per person before drinks, another Gault&Millau page EUR 185-520; Mes Prestiges gives lunch from EUR 175 and dinner from EUR 490 (seen Oct 2026)
reservation: Book well ahead; lunch is the easier seating to get
notes: The house was built on the chaud-froid d'oeuf, the "Arpège egg": a warm farm-egg yolk under cold four-spice cream sharpened with sherry vinegar and chives, a thread of maple, served in its own shell. Verify before you count on it — the July 2025 plant-based turn stripped eggs, cream and butter, so what reaches the table now is the garden: vegetables, fruit, herbs and flowers from Passard's own plots in the Sarthe and by Mont-Saint-Michel.
verdict: One of the most influential kitchens in modern Paris, and you can trace the bloodline: alumni run Septime (Bertrand Grébaut trained here) and Le Servan (Tatiana Levha, ex-Arpège, ex-Astrance). In July 2025 Passard went further than anyone at his level, striking meat, fish, shellfish, dairy and eggs from the menu — the first three-star in the world to do it, with only honey from his own hives surviving. Come for the vegetables off his own gardens, not for value, and not for the egg you've read about.
caveat: Not a value eat, and the prices quoted in 2026 sources disagree widely, so ask when you book. Since July 2025 the animal cooking that made Passard's name, the lobster and the pigeon, is gone, and so is the famous egg: the kitchen is all-vegetable but for the honey from its own hives. Portions can feel small for the money, and a table is hard-won.

name: Plénitude - Cheval Blanc Paris
address: Cheval Blanc Paris, 8 Quai du Louvre, 75001 Paris
tier: LA CRÈME — THE THREE-STAR HOUSES
recognition: Three MICHELIN stars since March 2022, kept in the Guide MICHELIN France 2026; No. 14 on The World's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 (the 2026 list is announced 4 November 2026 in Lima).
what_to_order: Langoustine, sabayon Cardinal Thenors|Turbot Tellurienne d'Hiver|Symphonie|Maxime Frédéric's desserts
notes: The sauces themselves. Donckele works as a self-styled saucier-parfumeur, numbering his layered sauces like perfumes into what he calls his "Absolues," and the two carte-blanche menus (Fuguons ensemble in 4 acts, Symphonie in 6) are built so that langoustine, turbot or pigeon serve as condiments to their broths, vinaigrettes and jus - named plates like La Langoustine Sabayon Cardinal Thenors and Turbot Tellurienne d'Hiver, reported by Fine Dining Lovers. Pastry by Maxime Frédéric, named World's Best Pastry Chef 2025.
verdict: Donckele's second three-star kitchen, and one that lived up to its billing rather than coasting on the Cheval Blanc name: three MICHELIN stars in barely seven months - awarded at the March 2022 Cognac ceremony, straight from zero to three - and held every year since, through the 2026 guide, backed by Gault&Millau 19/20 (five toques) and No. 14 on the World's 50 Best 2025. Here the sauce, not the protein, is the dish.
caveat: Not a discovery, a summit - and priced like one. The six-act Symphonie ran EUR 480 in 2025 (the four-act Fuguons ensemble EUR 445), with wine pairings up to EUR 495 on top; dinner only, Tuesday to Saturday, in a hushed 26-seat room above the Seine. The sauce-as-hero concept is cerebral and formal by design - go for the thrill of watching a master saucier work, not for comfort food or a casual night.

name: Kei
tier: LA CRÈME — THE THREE-STAR HOUSES
recognition: Three MICHELIN stars since 2020, retained in the 2026 Guide — Kei Kobayashi was the first Japanese chef to earn three stars in France.
what_to_order: Jardin de légumes croquants|Langoustine smoked over binchotan|Pigeon lacquered with red miso
price_range: Call ahead: Gault&Millau 2026 gives EUR 195-580 per person before drinks; Yonder (Jan 2026) menus from EUR 185; Mes Prestiges lunch about EUR 140, dinner EUR 310-380 (seen Oct 2026)
reservation: Online; bookings open on the first Tuesday of each month, two months ahead (old record), and fill fast
notes: Le jardin de légumes croquants — a "garden" of up to forty seasonal ingredients, crisp raw vegetables and herbs layered over Scottish smoked salmon, bound with a rocket cream and tomato vinaigrette and crowned with a cloud of lemon foam and a black-olive-and-almond crumble. It took five years to perfect and shifts with the season, so no two plates are quite alike.
verdict: France's only Japanese-born three-star chef, and the room has held all three MICHELIN stars every year since 2020 — this is precision plated as spectacle, not comfort or improvisation.
caveat: Ceremony and expense, not a spontaneous dinner: 2026 sources give menus from about EUR 185 up to EUR 580 and disagree on which runs at lunch, so confirm when you book. The room is small and books out.

name: Table by Bruno Verjus
tier: THE NEW HAUTE — THE PRODUCE AND THE FIRE
recognition: Bruno Verjus has announced Table's final service for 22 December 2026. It still holds two MICHELIN stars and was No. 8 on The World's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 (No. 3 in 2024).
what_to_order: Lobster mi-cru mi-cuit|Chocolate and caper tart with caviar|Couleur du jour
price_range: Couleur du jour menu EUR 480 before drinks (Sortiraparis, updated 9 Sept 2026; seen Oct 2026)
reservation: Book now if at all: one set seating, non-refundable deposit at booking, last service 22 December 2026
notes: Lobster 'mi-cru mi-cuit' — half-raw, half-cooked, trap-caught off the Ile d'Yeu, the shells toasted and the flesh warmed in ghee to roughly the temperature of the mouth — the dish critics reach for first when they describe him. The meal ends, as it always does, on his chocolate-and-caper tart under a spoon of caviar.
verdict: The two MICHELIN stars and the No. 8-in-the-world ranking are earned, not hype: one daily seating at a wave-shaped counter, Verjus plating in front of you, ingredient-worship over technique for its own sake. Book it and you'll watch a self-taught ex-food-critic cook the day's tide and fields into a single 'Couleur du jour' tasting.
caveat: Closing for good: the last service is 22 December 2026. One fixed tasting, no a la carte, at a counter of about two dozen seats, EUR 480 before drinks; expect the final weeks to be the hardest tables in Paris to land.

name: Datil
tier: THE NEW HAUTE — THE PRODUCE AND THE FIRE
recognition: 1 MICHELIN Star (2024) and MICHELIN Green Star (2026)
what_to_order: Peelings bouillon|Plum-stone tisane|Seven-course dinner tasting
price_range: Call ahead: lunch EUR 90-95, dinner about EUR 140; Gault&Millau gives EUR 95-160 before drinks (seen Oct 2026)
reservation: Book ahead; small room, tasting menu only
notes: The zero-waste tasting menu: it opens with a bouillon drawn from vegetable peelings (potato peel, at last report) and closes with a tisane brewed from plum stones — a nod to the restaurant's name. Plants lead; meat plays a background extra.
verdict: One of Paris's clearest proofs that a near-meatless tasting menu can carry a MICHELIN star — and, since 2026, a Green Star — without a single luxury crutch: no caviar, no wagyu, no truffle-for-show, animal protein used only as a condiment.
caveat: Tasting menu only, and the prices have climbed: 2026 sources range from about EUR 90 at lunch to EUR 160 at dinner (seen Oct 2026), so confirm when you book.

name: Le Rigmarole
tier: THE NEW HAUTE — THE PRODUCE AND THE FIRE
product_tags: Binchotan yakitori x handmade Italian pasta
recognition: Held one MICHELIN star from the 2020 guide; it was among the one-star removals in the 2023 France guide (Gilles Pudlowski, March 2023). Still carried on the World's 50 Best Discovery directory.
what_to_order: Spaghetti with bottarga|Yakitori thigh with clementine zest|Grilled oyster|Meatball
reservation: Book weeks ahead (listings suggest about six weeks for weekends, four for a Tuesday)
notes: Spaghetti with bottarga: house-made pasta under a snow of grated cured mullet roe. Its charcoal-side twin is the yakitori "thigh," perfumed with clementine zest.
verdict: A walnut counter where Robert Compagnon grills yakitori over Japanese binchotan while Jessica Yang's kitchen rolls the pasta by hand. It held a MICHELIN star from 2020 until the 2023 guide; the spaghetti with bottarga is still the plate regulars come back for, and the counter seats are few.
caveat: Small counter plus a few tables, tasting-menu driven and not cheap. Its MICHELIN star (awarded 2020) was withdrawn in the 2023 guide per Gilles Pudlowski's list of removals, so do not book it as a starred table. No 2026 review or post found: check it is trading before you plan around it.

name: Le Grand Véfour
tier: THE GRAND ROOMS — DATED
recognition: Gault&Millau 2026: 14/20 with a 'Table de Chef' mention for Bruno Doucet's relaunch. No MICHELIN star; the house held three from 2000 to 2008 and two until the 2021 guide.
what_to_order: Gigot d'agneau de lait|Soufflé glacé au Grand Marnier|Label Rouge gambas|Bar fillet
notes: Gigot d'agneau de lait carved tableside and a soufflé glacé au Grand Marnier — anchors of Bruno Doucet's pleasure-first, tableside-service menu (Elite Traveler; Les Nouvelles Gastronomiques, 2026). The old-era emblem, Guy Martin's ravioles de foie gras "Prince Vladimir," retired with him at the end of 2025.
verdict: A listed eighteenth-century room under the Palais-Royal arcades, where the banquettes still carry brass plaques for Napoléon, Victor Hugo and Colette. Paris Society reopened it on 12 May 2026 with Bruno Doucet's pleasure-first French menu and a garden terrace; Gault&Millau 2026 rates it 14/20. Go for the room and the ghosts first.
caveat: No MICHELIN star since the 2021 guide, and the relaunch carries none; Gault&Millau 2026 rates it 14/20 'Table de Chef'. A la carte only, no fixed menu. One listing (Mes Prestiges) names a different chef, Shintaro Awa, against Gault&Millau, Le Figaro and Paris Match naming Doucet, so confirm when you book. Come for the listed room and the garden terrace.
hot_this_month: On rue de Beaujolais under the Palais-Royal arcades: a fitting room for a Beaujolais Nouveau lunch on Thu 19 Nov 2026 (checked 16 Oct 2026).

name: Guy Savoy
address: 11 quai de Conti, 75006 Paris, France (Monnaie de Paris / Hotel de la Monnaie)
tier: THE GRAND ROOMS — DATED
recognition: Joint No. 1 restaurant in the world in La Liste 2026, its ninth consecutive year at the top. MICHELIN cut it to two stars in 2023; Yonder (January 2026) gives two stars.
what_to_order: Soupe d'artichaut à la truffe noire|Truffled brioche|Peas and lobster
price_range: Call ahead: Gault&Millau 2026 gives EUR 295-760 on one page and EUR 480-740 on another; Yonder (Jan 2026) lists a menu at EUR 740 (seen Oct 2026)
notes: Soupe d'artichaut a la truffe noire — artichoke and black-truffle soup, served with a toasted mushroom-and-truffle brioche slicked in black-truffle butter; his longest-standing signature and the plate most often named as his defining dish.
verdict: Two MICHELIN stars (down from three in 2023), yet joint No. 1 on La Liste 2026: a grand classical restaurant inside the Monnaie de Paris, the old royal mint, where the tasting menu still opens with the artichoke and black-truffle soup that has anchored his cooking for decades. The menu now runs to about EUR 740 (seen Jan 2026).
caveat: The "3 stars" billing is out of date: MICHELIN cut it to two in 2023 (it had held three since 2002) and has not restored the third. Its "world's best" standing comes from La Liste's algorithmic aggregator — and in 2026 that top spot is shared with nine other restaurants, all scoring 99.5/100 — not a single live-judged verdict. Dinner is a special-occasion outlay (roughly EUR 490 before wine); open only Wednesday to Saturday, with Saturday dinner-only.
hot_this_month: Autumn suits the signature artichoke and black-truffle soup with its truffle-butter brioche; La Liste joint No. 1 for 2026, two MICHELIN stars (checked 16 Oct 2026).

name: Le Train Bleu
address: Place Louis Armand, 75012 Paris (1st floor, Gare de Lyon, Hall 1)
tier: THE GRAND ROOMS — DATED
recognition: Gault&Millau: 12/20, "Table Gourmande" — "Institution nationale, Le Train Bleu est autant une bonne brasserie qu'un monument," where Rostang "sans prendre trop de risque, assure sa partition" (fr.gaultmillau.com, 2025).
what_to_order: Gigot d'agneau rôti|Crêpes Suzette|Baba au rhum|Quenelle de brochet, sauce Newburg
price_range: Call ahead: Time Out lists set menus at EUR 56, 70 and 98; Paris-friendly lists Menu du Voyageur EUR 57, PLM EUR 78, Train Bleu EUR 120 (+ wine EUR 42) (seen Oct 2026, both undated)
notes: Gigot d'agneau rôti — leg of lamb carved tableside from the trolley, with gratin dauphinois: the Train Bleu's tableside signature, kept on the card by Rostang. Crêpes Suzette, flambéed tableside, to finish.
verdict: You come for the room, not the plate. The gilded 1901 dining room above Gare de Lyon — 41 painted panels and crystal chandeliers — was classified a monument historique in 1972, and it is the real event. The food, Michel Rostang's traditional brasserie repertoire since October 2018, is competent and deliberately safe: Gault&Millau rates it 12/20, "Table Gourmande," not a destination kitchen.
caveat: Come for the Belle Époque room, not the cooking. Paris Unlocked found it "a bit safe" and "not always particularly inventive," with the pike-quenelle's Newburg sauce "curiously lacking in creaminess." Prices track the setting, not the kitchen.

name: Septime
tier: THE NEO-BISTRO LINE — THE 11TH
recognition: No. 40 on The World's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 (the 2026 list is announced 4 November 2026 in Lima); one MICHELIN star, held since 2014.
what_to_order: Carte blanche|Cèpes and girolles in peppercorn sauce|Young leeks in mussel and pimentón butter, lardo
reservation: Online only; a May 2026 review says the window opens 21 days out at 10:00 Paris time and fills in minutes, another source says one month ahead
notes: No fixed signature dish, by design: the carte blanche tasting menu is the whole offer, five steps at lunch, seven at dinner, driven by a near-obsessive micro-seasonality. Recent plates cited by The World's 50 Best: cepes and girolles in peppercorn sauce, and young leeks in a mussel-and-pimenton butter under wafer-thin lardo.
verdict: One MICHELIN star and No. 40 on The World's 50 Best 2025, and lunch is a carte blanche you do not choose: the kitchen sends what the week's harvest decides. The neo-bistro that set the template for a generation of Paris kitchens, in its first season without its founding chef, and still one of the hardest of them to book.
caveat: Chef-founder Bertrand Grébaut died in July 2026; who now leads the kitchen was not found, so the cooking you read about may change. No a la carte, carte blanche only. Booking is the hard part, and service days differ by source.
hot_this_month: The seasonal menu's moment: The World's 50 Best has cited its cèpes and girolles in peppercorn sauce, and October is cèpe season; book weeks out (checked 16 Oct 2026).

name: Le Servan
tier: THE NEO-BISTRO LINE — THE 11TH
recognition: Named Meilleur Bistrot 2015 by Le Fooding. A Mes Prestiges listing claims a MICHELIN star in 2026; no MICHELIN source confirms it.
what_to_order: Wontons de boudin noir, sauce chili doux|Mussels with chili and Thai basil|Lobster ravioli with Sichuan pepper|Tartare with peanuts and Thai chili
reservation: Book ahead; one listing says bookings open about a month out and fill quickly
notes: Wontons de boudin noir, sauce chili doux (blood-sausage wontons, sweet chili) — the house zakouski, a standout singled out by The Infatuation and given its own dish page by Paris by Mouth.
verdict: Go at lunch or for the late-afternoon zakouski and order the boudin-noir wontons under sweet chili and the chili-and-Thai-basil mussels; if the sauces and jus don't read as three-star discipline scaled down to bistro plates, the ex-Arpege / ex-Astrance pedigree is a line on a menu, not a kitchen.
caveat: No new find: a twelve-year-old (opened spring 2014), hard-to-book institution whose Le Fooding best-bistro crown dates to 2015. The room seats under 40, and the 2026 listings disagree on its days (one gives closed Sunday and Monday, Saturday dinner only): call before you go.

name: Clown Bar
tier: THE NEO-BISTRO LINE — THE 11TH
recognition: Reviewed by The Infatuation (Dec 2016) and called the most thrilling restaurant in Paris by Eater the same year; carried on World's 50 Best Discovery as a directory listing. Press signal is real but dated.
what_to_order: Cervelle de veau, bouillon dashi|Duck and foie gras pithivier
reservation: Book about two weeks ahead; walk-ins rarely land a seat
notes: Cervelle de veau: poached veal brain in a chilled dashi/ponzu broth finished with finely diced ginger and scallion. Added by Atsumi in 2014 and, by every account, the permanent fixture on an otherwise rotating card. The duck-and-foie-gras pithivier — breast, leg and foie gras in a caramelised crust — is the other order-it dish.
verdict: Order the cervelle de veau in chilled dashi — the one plate that never leaves the constantly-changing menu — and you eat Sota Atsumi's decade-old signature beneath a Sarreguemines ceramic clown frieze classé monument historique since 1995.
caveat: Two honest asterisks. The dining room is genuinely tiny and books out, so walk-ins rarely land a seat, and at bistro-plus prices with an offal-forward menu (brain, sweetbreads) this is a splurge, not a casual drop-in. And to correct the brief: Clown Bar is not on The Infatuation's current Best Bistros in Paris guide — its Infatuation review and Eater rave both date to 2016, so the press signal is real but aged.

name: Bistrot Paul Bert
tier: THE BISTRO CANON
recognition: On No Reservations, Anthony Bourdain called it one of the best of the old-school, unchanged-by-time Parisian bistros. A 2026 listing claims a Bib Gourmand; no MICHELIN source confirms it.
what_to_order: Steak au poivre|Gougères|Paris-Brest
reservation: Phone only; persist, it is hard to get through
notes: Steak au poivre - a thick cut of beef crusted in coarsely cracked Sarawak pepper and finished in a cognac-cream sauce, with crisp frites; complimentary gougeres to open and a Paris-Brest to close.
verdict: Still the dino-classic Paris bistrot Anthony Bourdain loved: the steak au poivre - coarse Sarawak pepper pressed into a thick cut of beef, finished in a cognac-cream sauce with crisp frites - is why you come, opened with complimentary gougeres and closed with a Paris-Brest. Falsifiable: it's phone-only and genuinely hard to land, closed Sunday and Monday, the room now runs heavily international, and at about 44 euros the steak divides critics on value - The Infatuation calls the branded merch and truffle-on-everything "a money grab."
caveat: Reservations are by phone only and genuinely hard to land - the kitchen largely stopped answering the phone in fall 2022 as Bourdain-era demand overwhelmed it, and Paris by Mouth dropped it from its recommendations over the reservation chaos; the room now runs heavily international. In The Infatuation (Emily Monaco, 2024) the cooking still wins, but she flags the branded sweatshirts and truffle-on-everything as feeling like "a money grab"; on her own blog the same critic rates it good yet no better than similarly priced bistros such as Chez Georges. Steak au poivre runs about 44 euros. Closed Sunday and Monday.

name: Chez L'Ami Jean
tier: THE BERTHS · THE BISTRO CANON
recognition: Gault&Millau 2026: 13/20, two toques, 'still reliable' though 'a little on autopilot'. The Infatuation's Best Bistros in Paris guide (9 June 2026, per the old record) also lists it.
what_to_order: Riz au lait|Roast grouse|Wild boar stew
reservation: Reserve well ahead; tables are tight
notes: Riz au lait — vanilla rice pudding served tableside in a large bowl with salted-butter caramel sauce and housemade nougatine on the side to assemble your own
verdict: A fixture on The Infatuation's "The Best Bistros In Paris." Order the riz au lait: it arrives as one big bowl for the table, the salted-butter caramel and housemade nougatine in separate dishes for you to fold in yourself. In autumn and winter, wild game — roast grouse, wild boar stew — is the reason to book.
caveat: Loud, cramped and expensive — The Infatuation's top ($$$$) tier: the sensory overload is the whole point, not a quiet or budget meal. Game is strictly seasonal (autumn–winter), so out of season you won't find it, and tables are tight — reserve well ahead.
hot_this_month: Game season is open: the record gives autumn and winter wild game, roast grouse and wild boar stew, as the reason to book; reserve ahead (checked 16 Oct 2026).

name: Chez Georges
tier: THE BISTRO CANON
recognition: The Infatuation ($$$$): a time-warp bistro with a handwritten menu, Jean-Gabriel de Bueil its 'committed guardian' (review dated 18 March 2026 per the old record; date not re-seen). Gault&Millau 11/20.
what_to_order: Foie de veau|Salade lyonnaise|Escargots|Pan-roasted chicken
reservation: No online booking: call, email or go in person
notes: Foie de veau - a thick slab of calf's liver - served beside a mound of shoestring frites, after the escargots and a shared bowl of salade lyonnaise heavy with thumb-sized lardons.
verdict: Old-Paris kept exactly where it was: on rue du Mail since 1964, the menu still handwritten in looping French script, the salade lyonnaise still arriving as a shared bowl heavy with thumb-sized lardons, the foie de veau still landing beside a mound of shoestring frites. Lunch and dinner on weekdays only - dark every Saturday and Sunday, and closed for the August holidays. Weekday, or not at all.
caveat: Not cheap and not cuddly. The Infatuation rates it $$$$ and calls the wine list "ultimately overpriced," with service that blends "efficiency, practiced scorn, and flirtiness." There is no online booking - you call, re-call, email, or turn up in person - and beware the several unrelated Paris restaurants that share the name (one of them a vegetarian spot); only rue du Mail is this one.

name: Le Baratin
tier: THE WINE BISTROS — THE CELLAR FIRST
recognition: Time Out Paris: pastry chef Pierre Hermé visits 'at least every two weeks'; Hermé told Purepeople (23 Dec 2025) he has been coming for nearly 30 years. Time Out rates it 4/5.
what_to_order: Cervelle de veau au beurre citronné|Terrine de museau de porc|Oreilles de cochon croustillantes|Braise of the day|Natural wine by the glass
reservation: Book by phone a day or two ahead
notes: Cervelle de veau — poached calf's brain in lemon butter, the most-cited plate on a daily-changing blackboard that also runs to pork-snout terrine, crispy pig's ears and braised meats.
verdict: Belleville's benchmark natural-wine bistrot: a daily blackboard of offal-forward, deeply personal cooking that Paris food writers credit Raquel Carena with pioneering — bistronomie before it had a name — paired to one of the city's deepest natural-wine cellars (20-plus by the glass, independent-focused). If you want polish, comfort and a warm greeting, this isn't it; if you want the real, unreconstructed thing, it is.
caveat: The welcome is the running joke: reviewers warn the front of house can be brusque, The Infatuation (2024) describing an almost comically ornery maître d', and Time Out admitting it has not always found the service the friendliest. The room is small and the blackboard changes daily.

name: Parcelles
tier: THE WINE BISTROS — THE CELLAR FIRST
recognition: Gault&Millau 2026: 13/20, calling five years on rue Chapon an ode to bistronomy; Time Out 4/5 (Sept 2025); Opinionated About Dining Casual Europe No. 167 (2025, per Enprimeurclub).
what_to_order: Ris de veau au beurre noisette|Carpaccio de tête de veau|Gnocchi au beurre de sauge|A bottle from the shop opposite
price_range: Call ahead: Paris Eater lists starters about EUR 19-24, mains EUR 39-45, desserts about EUR 13; Lesrestos estimates EUR 30-50 a head (seen Oct 2026)
reservation: Book dinner weeks ahead (Paris Eater)
notes: Ris de veau au beurre noisette (veal sweetbreads in brown butter, with pommes purée) — the plate most consistently singled out across reviews (Time Out 2025, Gault&Millau, and the restaurant's own listings) — though the menu is chalked on a slate and rotates daily with the market, so treat it as emblematic rather than guaranteed.
verdict: Not the unranked newcomer the "hot table" framing suggests. Five years open (since spring 2021), Parcelles is an established Haut-Marais standard: Time Out still scores it 4/5 and keeps it "on the podium of Paris's best bistros" (Sept 2025), Gault&Millau marks it 13/20, and it holds a Le Fooding listing plus a place in the MICHELIN Guide selection (a plate — no Bib or star). The daily plates back the cellar rather than hiding behind it.
caveat: The slate changes daily, so no dish is guaranteed. Closed weekends. Gault&Millau 2026 names Julien Chevallier as chef; Time Out has named Emmanuel Perrot, so confirm who is cooking before quoting a name. Mains near EUR 40 put it well above bistro prices.

name: Vantre
address: 19 rue de la Fontaine au Roi, 75011 Paris
tier: THE WINE BISTROS — THE CELLAR FIRST
recognition: Wine Spectator Grand Award, first won 2019; 2025's new Paris Grand Award went to Le Bon Georges, and Vantre's current listing was not re-checked. Gault&Millau 2026: 13/20 with a Table de Chef mention.
what_to_order: Gnocchi in sage butter|A bottle from the list
notes: Gnocchi in sage butter
verdict: The cooking is precise and reliably good, but the reason Vantre matters is the cellar: a list that first won a Wine Spectator Grand Award in 2019, in a room this small, and the rare place to drink at that depth without a fine-dining bill.
caveat: No MICHELIN star or Bib; the Guide lists it. The kitchen has changed hands three times (Chomel, Nagao, Satria Vue since 2023), so the food is less constant than the wine. About 30 seats, weekdays only; book ahead. Cellar figures vary: Gault&Millau says over 3,000 wines, Le Fooding about 5,000 bottles, Wine Spectator far more in the cellar.

name: Brasserie Lipp
tier: THE BRASSERIES — DATED
recognition: Gault&Millau 2026: 12/20 with a Table Gourmande mention; menu barely changed since the 1950s. The Infatuation (Feb 2025): 'you're here for the legend.'
what_to_order: Choucroute garnie|Sole meunière|Andouillette|Blanquette de veau|Mille-feuille
reservation: Book ahead for weekend evenings; walk-ins risky on busy nights (Mes Prestiges, May 2026)
notes: Choucroute garnie — wine-braised sauerkraut with sausages, bacon and steamed potatoes; the house dish since 1880, when the original starter was cervelat rémoulade.
verdict: The food is not the reason to come, and no one honest pretends otherwise. Order the choucroute garnie, take a ground-floor table, and you are eating inside the Saint-Germain of Verlaine, Apollinaire, Hemingway and Mitterrand. Checkable on the ground: the waiters still wear numbered seniority pins, the 1900 dining room is a protected monument historique, and the upstairs is nicknamed l'Enfer — hell, where you are sent to be forgotten.
caveat: Not a food pilgrimage. The Infatuation (Feb 2025) found the cooking heavy and short on flavour complexity — "Between the heaviness of the meal and the lack of flavor complexity, they're fine… ultimately, you're here for the legend." It reads as a tourist-supported institution; the seating is a class system (ground-floor main room best, the back room is Purgatoire, the upstairs is Enfer), and the house posts signs about proper attire at the door. No MICHELIN star — the signal is journalistic and historical, not gastronomic.
hot_this_month: The choucroute garnie at a ground-floor table is the cold-evening order; an easy walk from the Musée d'Orsay and its Cassatt show (checked 16 Oct 2026).

name: Bofinger
phone: +33 1 42 72 87 82 (listing site; not checked against own site)
tier: THE BRASSERIES — DATED
recognition: The Infatuation (16 Apr 2025): 'Bofinger is the prototypical brasserie, with a stunning seafood menu that matches the grandeur of the space.'
what_to_order: Choucroute de la mer|Choucroute garnie|Plateau de fruits de mer
notes: Choucroute de la mer — salmon, haddock, sea bream (daurade) and a prawn fanned around a mound of juniper-and-cumin sauerkraut under a horseradish-spiked beurre blanc (the classic pork choucroute garnie and the fruits de mer seafood tower are the other house anchors).
verdict: The oldest Alsatian brasserie in Paris (est. 1864) and, by its own well-repeated claim, the first in the city to pour draught beer (1870); its facades, sign and interior decor — the floral Art Nouveau glass dome and the Gambrinus stained glass among them — have been a listed monument historique since 13 March 1989 (inscrit MH partiellement, per the official Merimee record), and the choucroute, seafood or classic, is still the reason to book.
caveat: A 280-seat, tourist-heavy group brasserie (Groupe Bertrand since its 2017 takeover of Groupe Flo); service, noise and value split diners. The 'first draught beer in Paris' line is house lore. Olivier Nasti's 2023 residency (30 March-31 May) is over; he does not run the kitchen.
hot_this_month: Choucroute weather from the clocks going back on 25 Oct: the oldest Alsatian brasserie in Paris, est. 1864, near the Bastille (checked 16 Oct 2026).

name: La Coupole
tier: THE BRASSERIES — DATED
recognition: Time Out Paris rates it 3/5: 'the grandest of grand Parisian brasseries', a classic experience without spending too much. Ground-floor room inscrit monument historique, 12 Jan 1988.
what_to_order: Curry d'agneau à l'indienne|Vegetarian curry|Oysters and seafood platters
price_range: Time Out lists mains EUR 27-36 and set menus EUR 29 and 34 (page undated; seen Oct 2026)
reservation: Recommended; it gets very busy
notes: Curry d'Agneau a l'Indienne — the house lamb curry, on the menu since 1927 and said to follow a Madras recipe; long served tableside "a la roulotte" and plated with rice and a spread of condiments (mango chutney, achars). The finer garnish details vary by telling, so take them lightly.
verdict: You come for the room, not the cooking: the 1927 dining hall, its pillars hand-painted by 27 artists, has its ground-floor room listed (inscrit) as a monument historique by order of 12 January 1988, and the one dish worth ordering is the Curry d'Agneau, on the menu essentially unchanged since opening day. Verify by walking in: read the columns, then the carte.
caveat: This is an institution living partly on its legend. Curated reviews (The Infatuation, Paris-Bistro) are candid that the food is competent-but-unremarkable grand-brasserie fare and that you are paying for the setting and the history; service can visibly buckle under big group tables at peak. Treat it as a story and a room first, a meal second — and note the fabled "Mitterrand's last meal" curry line is repeated lore, not documented fact (what is documented is that Mitterrand kept table 82 and ordered the curry).

name: Bouillon Chartier
tier: THE BOUILLONS AND THE CRÉMERIE — CHEAP SINCE THE 1800S
recognition: Named in the MICHELIN Guide's editorial feature 'The Return of Brasseries and Bouillons in Paris' among the city's landmark bouillons, alongside Bouillon Julien and Bouillon Pigalle — an editorial mention, not a star rating.
what_to_order: Oeuf mayonnaise|Boeuf bourguignon|Steak frites, sauce poivre|Profiteroles au chocolat
price_range: Call ahead: one guide gives starters from about EUR 1, mains from EUR 7, desserts from EUR 2; another puts a main around EUR 15 (seen Oct 2026)
reservation: No reservations; queue
notes: The emblematic cheap opener is the œuf mayonnaise, ordered in loose change; bœuf bourguignon and steak frites (pièce du boucher, sauce poivre, frites) are the house mains, with the chocolate profiterole — called Chartier's crown jewel — the long-running favourite to finish.
verdict: A real 1896 broth canteen, not a themed reproduction: strangers still share communal tables under globe lamps while bow-tied waiters tot up the bill on the paper tablecloth, inside a hall whose décor has been classé monument historique since 1989. Mains sit in the low tens of euros — you come for the room and the almost-anachronistic price, not for cooking that would trouble a star.
caveat: It is a tourist institution that feeds hundreds at a clip: expect a queue at the Grands Boulevards flagship (no reservations — first-come, first-served), brisk-to-rushed service, and simple, sometimes uneven cooking. Treat it as living heritage and a genuine bargain, not a destination meal.

name: Polidor
tier: THE BOUILLONS AND THE CRÉMERIE — CHEAP SINCE THE 1800S
recognition: Gault&Millau's current online listing scores Polidor 11/20 and calls it a mythical, preserved 'slice of Paris' serving bistro classics revisited for the 21st century, singling out the chocolate mousse; the modest score is itself the tell.
what_to_order: Boeuf bourguignon|Le semainier|Mousse au chocolat|Tarte Tatin|House wine by the pichet
price_range: EUR 15.90-25 a head before drinks (Gault&Millau 2026; seen Oct 2026)
notes: Boeuf bourguignon, the emblematic slow-braised bistro main, cheap and generously portioned; for dessert, Gault&Millau singles out the chocolate mousse, with tarte Tatin the other house classic on the menu (Gault&Millau; restaurant menu).
verdict: A living Belle Epoque dining room, not a great kitchen. The boeuf bourguignon and chocolate mousse are honest, generous and cheap, but the ceiling is real: Gault&Millau stops at 11/20 and plates can arrive lukewarm. Come for permanence and the literary ghosts, not for cooking that changes your mind.
caveat: This is sincerity, not spectacle, and the record is genuinely mixed: cooking that can land lukewarm and inconsistent, and brisk, no-nonsense service. It has been tourist-heavy since the 2011 film, seating is elbow-to-elbow at communal tables with shared salt, pepper and mustard, and the WC is still a Turkish squat. You are paying for the room and the history more than the plate.

name: Bouillon Pigalle
phone: +33 1 42 59 69 31 (Mes Prestiges; not checked against own site)
tier: THE BOUILLONS AND THE CRÉMERIE — CHEAP SINCE THE 1800S
recognition: Its oeuf mayonnaise was named world champion by the ASOM jury in June 2019; Gault&Millau 2026: a correct meal for about EUR 20; featured in MICHELIN's bouillon-revival article (editorial, no star or Bib).
what_to_order: Oeuf mayonnaise|Boeuf bourguignon|Terrine de canard|Île flottante|Profiteroles
price_range: About EUR 20 a head (Gault&Millau 2026; seen Oct 2026)
reservation: Call ahead: Privateaser takes online bookings (groups over 12 by email or phone); Mes Prestiges (May 2026) says it runs mostly walk-in
notes: Oeuf mayonnaise: the plain egg and mayonnaise whose recipe, under chef Clément Chicard, was crowned world champion by the ASOM jury in June 2019.
verdict: Order the oeuf mayo, a beef bourguignon (EUR 12.20 by Gault&Millau 2026) and profiteroles, add a pichet, and you are around EUR 20 to 25 a head in a 300-seat room on the boulevard de Clichy.
caveat: Go for the room, the roar and the arithmetic, not for finesse. This is cooking that is generous, not precise: competent bistro classics turned out at canteen speed for a 300-seat room. It now takes bookings for parties of two to twelve — a break from its walk-in-only start — but the queue down boulevard de Clichy is still real after 7pm, and on an off night it reads more tourist crush than neighbourhood table.

name: Clamato
tier: WALK IN BY DAY — THE SEAFOOD BAR AND THE DAY KITCHEN
recognition: MICHELIN Bib Gourmand, listed under the France 2026 selection (Mes Prestiges extract; Pearl dates it 2025). MICHELIN's page: no reservations, first come, first served.
what_to_order: Couteaux, beurre d'herbes|Oysters from the raw bar|Accras de crabe|Plateau de fruits de mer|Tarte au sirop d'érable
reservation: None; first come, first served (MICHELIN)
notes: Couteaux, beurre d'herbes — razor clams in herb butter, finished with almonds. The catch changes with the morning's delivery, but the raw-bar oysters, crab accras, the fruits de mer platter (50 Best's "star of the show") and a Québécois maple-syrup pie are the constants.
verdict: The Septime team's raw bar is the 11e's benchmark for catch-of-the-day seafood, and it has never taken a booking since it opened in 2013 — turn up at the 7pm opening or after 10pm, or you queue for a stool.
caveat: No reservations, ever, and the room is small and shoulder-to-shoulder — expect to wait unless you arrive at opening or late. The menu is dictated by the day's catch, so any single dish may not be on; and while it wears a Bib Gourmand, platters and natural wine make the bill climb. Listed hours conflict across sources (some show closures early in the week) — verify before going.
hot_this_month: R-month oyster season: the raw-bar oysters and the fruits de mer platter are the order; no bookings, so queue at opening (checked 16 Oct 2026).

name: Mokonuts
tier: WALK IN BY DAY — THE SEAFOOD BAR AND THE DAY KITCHEN
product_tags: Weekday breakfast & lunch day kitchen - Franco-Levantine-Japanese
recognition: Paris by Mouth, 'Mokonuts, revisited' (2026): rated GREAT, on its 50 Favorites since the list began. The Infatuation (18 Mar 2026): 'flavor-packed and near-perfect.' Gault&Millau 12/20.
what_to_order: Black-olive and white-chocolate cookie|Peanut-butter and milk-chocolate cookie|Miso, black sesame or tahini cookies|Hake, pil-pil sauce, caramelised endive
reservation: Book weeks ahead; walk-ins near hopeless
notes: Moko Hirayama's cookies - American-style bakes rerouted through Japan with miso, black sesame and tahini (the black-olive-and-white-chocolate and peanut-butter-milk-chocolate are the cult orders, per Paris by Mouth and David Lebovitz); on the savory side, the short daily menu has run to hake with pil-pil sauce and caramelized endive (Paris by Mouth). The menu changes with the market.
verdict: A 20-seat, breakfast-and-lunch-only room open Monday to Friday since 2015, where Moko Hirayama runs the pastry and floor and Omar Koreitem cooks one short, market-driven Franco-Levantine menu. It holds no Michelin star and only a modest Gault&Millau 12/20 (2026) - the real signal is that it books up weeks in advance on critical praise alone.
caveat: Breakfast and lunch only, weekdays, and just 20 covers - it books up weeks ahead (The Infatuation lists it among Paris's toughest reservations), so walk-ins are near-hopeless. The Infatuation pegs it $$$$. If the table won't happen, come for the cookies.

name: L'As du Fallafel
tier: THE BERTHS · AT THE WINDOW — FALAFEL, THE SANDWICH, THE HAM
recognition: The Infatuation (8 Oct 2025): six falafel 'as green as the storefront' with fried eggplant and tahini. Mark Bittman (NYT): 'the falafel destination in Paris, indeed in Europe.'
what_to_order: Falafel special in pita|Fried aubergine
notes: The falafel special (pita): six crisp, herb-dense falafel balls so green they match the storefront, plus fried aubergine, tahini, hummus, cabbage and cucumber.
verdict: Order and pay at the green window before you even reach the front, then walk off with a fresh pita crammed with six herb-green falafel balls, silky fried aubergine, tahini, and shredded red-and-white cabbage - heavy as two fists, and the falafel every rival window on rue des Rosiers is measured against.
caveat: The queue is real and regularly spills into the street. It is kosher (Beth Din of Paris oversight) and therefore closed Friday evening, all day Saturday and on Jewish holidays for Shabbat, so plan around it. And the "best falafel" crown is genuinely contested: rue des Rosiers is now lined with rival windows all claiming it (Vice documented an outright "falafel war"), and the signal here is journalistic, not a MICHELIN or Gault&Millau ranking.

name: Chez Alain Miam Miam
address: 26 rue Charlot, 75003 Paris (the shop only; the former market stall is gone with the market)
tier: AT THE WINDOW — FALAFEL, THE SANDWICH, THE HAM
recognition: Reviewed by The Infatuation's Paris team: a Marche des Enfants Rouges original that moved to its own rue Charlot storefront, with a specific recommended build (smoky cecina, Cantal or Comte, tomato, caramelized onion, mushroom, toasted).
what_to_order: Cecina de León sandwich|Pastrami sandwich|Smoked trout sandwich|Buckwheat galette
price_range: From EUR 13.50 a sandwich (The Infatuation; seen Oct 2026)
notes: The oversized griddled sandwich: smoky cecina de Leon (or cooked/raw ham, pastrami, spiced chicken, smoked trout), Cantal or Comte, plus tomato, caramelized onion and mushroom, toasted to order. Buckwheat galettes round out the board.
verdict: A two-handed, overstuffed toasted sandwich, layered and pressed to order at the counter. Order the smoky cecina de Leon with Cantal (or Comte), the complimentary tomato, caramelized onion and mushroom, and have it toasted. Budget from 13.50 euros, plus roughly 25 minutes in line just to reach the counter.
caveat: The Marché des Enfants Rouges burned down on 11-12 October 2026 (Time Out Paris, AFP): do not go to the market. No report found on whether the rue Charlot shop is trading after the fire; call or check its social accounts first. When open: The Infatuation calls the EUR 13.50-plus sandwich overhyped and underseasoned, with about 25 minutes in line to order.

name: Le Petit Vendôme
tier: AT THE WINDOW — FALAFEL, THE SANDWICH, THE HAM
recognition: Time Out's 'best sandwiches in the world' (2025): No. 1, ahead of Epping Forest Oyster Shack and Kush Hialeah. David Lebovitz: 'the best sandwich in Paris.'
what_to_order: Jambon-beurre|Le Spécial|Plat du jour
notes: The jambon-beurre, plain, to read the bread, butter and ham balance; or the Spécial, with dry-cured country ham, fresh goat cheese and olive oil.
verdict: The genuine benchmark, not a tourist trap dressed as one: order it plain to judge it. The classic jambon-beurre runs about EUR 6.50 (AFP, Apr 2026), and it is closed on Sundays.
caveat: Since the Time Out ranking the queue is managed with barriers on the pavement; go early or late. Counter service, no reservations; closed Sunday.

name: Breizh Café
tier: ONE DISH, ONE ROOM — THE GALETTE AND THE STEAK
recognition: Cooks with Jean-Yves Bordier butter and IGP Breton buckwheat, with Cancale oysters and a long cider list; a Paris by Mouth favourite (old record, not re-checked).
what_to_order: Galette complète|Galette with Label Rouge smoked salmon|Crêpe au caramel beurre salé|Cancale oysters|Cider flight
reservation: Reserve ahead
notes: The Complète made with Bordier butter and organic buckwheat, or a galette with Label Rouge smoked salmon; finish with the salted-caramel crêpe and a regional cider flight.
verdict: The best-sourced galette in Paris, and priced like it. Falsifiable: it works with Jean-Yves Bordier butter and IGP Breton buckwheat, and unlike Josselin it takes reservations — which you'll want.
caveat: price/booking — pricier than a classic crêperie; reserve ahead.
hot_this_month: Oysters are back: the house serves Cancale oysters with its buckwheat galettes and cider, a good October lunch in the Marais (checked 16 Oct 2026).

name: La Crêperie de Josselin
tier: ONE DISH, ONE ROOM — THE GALETTE AND THE STEAK
recognition: Time Out Paris 3/5: a queue even on weekdays, generous if slightly greasy crêpes, a bill rarely above EUR 20.
what_to_order: Galette complète|Bolée de cidre brut|Crêpe caramel beurre salé
price_range: Rarely over EUR 20 a head (Time Out, undated; seen Oct 2026)
notes: La complète (ham, egg, Gruyère) with a bolée of cidre brut, then a salted-butter caramel crêpe to finish.
verdict: The most honest galette in the Breton quarter by Montparnasse: skip the flourishes and order the complète. No reservations, and the cider arrives in a ceramic bowl, not a glass; the listings disagree on its closing days, so check before you go.
caveat: No reservations, tight room, queue even on weekdays (Time Out). Closing days conflict across sources; check before crossing town. Time Out finds the crêpes generous but a little greasy.

name: Le Relais de l'Entrecôte
address: 20 rue Saint-Benoît, 75006 Paris (also 15 rue Marbeuf 8e, 101 bd du Montparnasse 14e)
tier: ONE DISH, ONE ROOM — THE GALETTE AND THE STEAK
recognition: One fixed menu since 1959: salad, then steak-frites in the guarded sauce, second helping included. Listed by Opinionated About Dining 2026 (casual), per a Pearl extract.
what_to_order: Walnut and lettuce salad|Contrefilet steak-frites
price_range: Call ahead: about EUR 30 in the old record; Frommer's (undated) gives a EUR 27 set menu (seen Oct 2026)
reservation: No reservations; queue
notes: There is no choice: a walnut-and-lettuce salad, then contrefilet steak-frites in the guarded herb-butter sauce, second serving included, about €30.
verdict: Not actually quick: a queue, then a full sit-down, a second helping of steak and frites included. No reservations, roughly EUR 30, and three Paris rooms (Saint-Benoît, Marbeuf, Montparnasse); the Marbeuf room was closed for works in 2026 and its reopening is unconfirmed, so this guide sends you to rue Saint-Benoît.
caveat: Not quick: a queue, then a full sit-down. No bookings. The Marbeuf branch's reopening (old record: about 28 July 2026) was not confirmed; check your branch. Not the same house as the Relais de Venise.
